text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- The number of poor has not increased in Sweden since 1994 but more people are close to poverty, a report shows. Immigrants and young people are the only groups whose situation has worsened.
- Real estate agents warn of euphoria similar to that of the 80s on the Stockholm market. Apartment and house prices have risen 10-15 percent this spring, building on a boom in the autumn of 1996.

- Swedish forestry companies are taking a wait-and-see attitude ahead of futures and derivates trader OM's plans to open a pulp exchange in London, PULPEX. Trade is scheduled to start on Thursday. But attempts to set up a pulp exchange in Helsinki and Vancouver have failed.

- A number of firms plan to move from the Stockholm Stock Exchange's main A list to a smaller O list because of changes to wealth tax that are expected to be approved in parliament today. The new law would give firms on the O list a tax advantage.

- Volvo is planning to set up a central business centre in Brussels which could have the head office for Volvo Construction Equipment, European marketing for the group, local purchasing units for Volvo cars and trucks and Volvo's European Union lobbying organisation.

- Rumours are rampant that the government is leaning towards closing the door to Europe's economic and monetary union possibly until 2002, the year of the next parliamentary election. "The market is already punishing the market everyday. We have a spread of 120 basis points against the mark and the Swedish economy looks good in other respects," said Mattias Sundling, an analyst at brokerage Hagstromer & Qviberg.
- Computer company Lap Power tops the growth list with a 48 percent increase in last year.
- The International Monetary Fund (IMF) recommends Sweden cut tax and reform the labour market but praises improved state finances.
